newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya says Uganda unable to meet power obligations.
newsitem.headline: Kenya says Uganda unable to meet power obligations.

text.p: Kenyan authorities said on Monday Uganda was unable to meet its power export obligations owing to its own fast-growing economy and Kenya had licensed two private companies to bridge its current electricity supply shortfall.
Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni complained at the weekend that Uganda exported 30 megawatts of power to Kenya at a loss under a contract signed more than half-a-century ago.
Museveni said he wanted a review and threatened to cut the supply to Kenya unless there was an urgent review of the rates.

In reaction, Kenyan Energy Minister Darius Mbela told reporters on Sunday that Kenya was willing to discuss a review of that contract because the current cost of power greatly exceeded the pricing in the 1940s when the contract was signed.

A spokesman at the Kenya Power & Lighting Company (KP&LC) told Reuters on Monday that the problem was not renegotiating the contract but a guarantee by Uganda that the 30 megawatts stipulated in the contract would indeed be exported to Kenya.

"Uganda's economy is expanding fast and it is difficult for them to export the power to Kenya at peak hours when we, like they, most need it," the spokesman said. "Right now, we simply do not get the 30 megawatts we expect. That is the problem."
Kenya Power & Lighting Company stock on the Nairobi Stock Exchange fell 3.0 shillings to 113 on the latest dispute.
According to the contract, Uganda exports power to Kenya at 20 Kenyan cents per unit, very low even by Kenyan standards.
"Uganda cannot meet its own power needs at peak hours. They want to supply to us when we do not need it, like at night, that's when we least need power," the KP&LC spokesman added.

Meantime the KP&LC spokesman confirmed that the company had awarded Sabah Shipyard, an Indonesian Company, and Ibera-Africa, a Spanish company, contracts to generate a total of 87.5 megawatts of electricity for the national grid.

The companies will generate electricity as a stop-gap measure to supplement national demand and will have their plants commissioned in two phases in February or March and May or June next year. But they must supply power by June, he said.

Sabah Shipyard will install a power barge at the port of Mombasa to generage 43 megawatts of power to be connected to the national grid at the Kipevu power station in the coastal area while Ibera-Africa will install a diesel plant in Nairobi to generate 44.5 megawatts, the spokesman said.
Sabah Shipyard and Ibera-Africa were selected from 15 companies after Kenya floated an international bid. No local investors were considered.
Kenya has a power deficit of about 50 megawatts. The system's peak demand is about 670 megawatts while current available capacity is 620 megawatts, according to the KP&LC.
A 75-megawatt thermal generating station, with funding from Japan, is unlikely to operate before 1999.
